target: AG1’s claim that AI is broadly good for society because it increases convenience, health, safety, productivity, accessibility, and opportunity.
objection: AI is not good for society overall; it tends to erode economic security, weaken critical thinking, intensify racial bias, and create serious privacy risks.

target: AG1’s assumption that routine-task automation mainly helps workers by freeing them for higher-value work.
objection: In practice, automation often displaces workers faster than it creates new opportunities, shifting costs and instability onto employees and small businesses rather than improving economic well-being.

target: AG1’s idea that AI can support learning without harming students’ reasoning skills.
objection: AI tools can replace practice and judgment, causing students and adults to rely on generated answers instead of developing the ability to evaluate evidence and reason independently.

target: AG1’s claim that AI benefits accessibility and safety without major downsides.
objection: AI systems can reproduce and amplify racial stereotypes from biased data, and they also require large-scale data collection that creates serious privacy and surveillance risks.

target: AG1’s argument that AI harms are not inevitable and can be solved through better design and governance.
objection: Those harms are structurally hard to prevent in real-world adoption, so mitigation is not reliable enough to change AI’s net effect from harmful to beneficial.

target: AG1’s claim that companies will use AI as augmentation and provide retraining so workers are protected.
objection: Business incentives reward cost reduction and speed, not worker stability, so companies are likely to automate faster than retraining can catch up, making “responsible adoption” an unreliable safeguard against labor-market harm.

target: AG1’s claim that AI can be used as a tutor or coach that improves critical thinking.
objection: Even if AI is presented as a coach, most users will treat it as an answer source under time pressure, which changes study habits and reduces verification and reasoning practice.

target: AG1’s claim that bias can be reduced through fairness testing, audits, improved datasets, and human review.
objection: Audits and fairness testing do not fully solve bias because models can generalize in opaque ways and bias can re-enter through new data, user behavior, and deployment contexts.

target: AG1’s claim that privacy risks can be reduced through data minimization, consent controls, and access limits.
objection: Commercial AI ecosystems often do not use such protections by default, and even privacy-preserving techniques can be undermined by scale and by inference of sensitive traits from seemingly harmless inputs.

target: AG1’s proposal that policy, incentives, and application design can make AI safe enough for society.
objection: Enforceable constraints do not scale reliably across fast-changing deployments, and the benefits and harms are distributed unevenly—large firms capture gains while many workers and small businesses absorb the shocks.

target: AG1’s claim that government or institutional rules can reliably enforce safe, fair AI deployment.
objection: Regulation often lags behind AI development, compliance becomes performative, and rules can be undermined by regulatory gaps, cross-border deployment, and corporate lobbying or capture.

target: AG1’s expectation that transition support will protect people harmed by automation.
objection: Even when productivity rises, gains often go to large firms and platform owners, while workers—especially racial minorities—bear the job loss, cost-cutting, and labor-market churn, so transition support will not reliably reach everyone harmed.

target: AG1’s belief that targeted deployment can keep AI benefits while avoiding harmful spillover.
objection: Once organizations adopt AI infrastructure, it tends to spread into other domains because it is profitable and easy to repurpose, so targeted deployment is not a durable guarantee against broader harm.

target: AG1’s claim that automation bias can be managed by presenting outputs with citations, uncertainty, and reasoning steps.
objection: Critical thinking erosion is hard to contractually prevent because users internalize AI outputs as authority under time pressure and competitive incentives, so they still take shortcuts despite such design features.

target: AG1’s claim that AI can help fight misinformation and manipulation through provenance, fact-checking, and monitoring.
objection: AI also amplifies persuasive text, audio, and video generation at scale, increasing misinformation, polarization, and manipulation in ways that cannot be fully bounded by per-application testing.

target: AG1’s claim that permissioned systems, restrictions, and monitoring can prevent harmful repurposing of AI tools.
objection: Those technical controls are fragile because attackers can spoof, remix, or synthesize outputs to bypass them, creating a constant arms race rather than stable protection.

target: AG1’s claim that requiring users to verify sources and show work will preserve learning and decision quality.
objection: This verification burden acts like a user tax, because it assumes people have time, literacy, and access to reliable sources; under pressure, most will still treat outputs as authoritative, so automation bias remains.

target: AG1’s claim that AI-based safety measures can counter misinformation without major new downsides.
objection: Safety auditing often requires more logging, monitoring, and training on large user and content datasets, which increases privacy risks and can intensify surveillance, especially for minorities with less power to contest it.
